inline.s: Praise of Great Being Guanyin of the Sea Tide

The myriad forms are universally sealed; the sea of nature is profoundly still. One gust of circumstance-wind, and the waves surge to the sky. The perfect Dharma body abides unmoved, serene and ever present; within the waves its radiance shines forth all the more. Therefore, when beings’ waves of consciousness do evil, the Dharma body lies hidden yet still becomes seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving. Therefore the wise, amid seeing and hearing, turn back their gaze in a single thought, and the sea of karma is suddenly emptied. The Great Being saves from suffering, yet comes not from without: it is the self-mind made manifest, wrought without contrivance. Since it is only the self-mind, why seek outside? Simply hearing the nature of hearing — this is named Guanyin.
Praise of Guanyin, the Sea Moon — a Great Being Seated Within the Full Moon in the Midst of the Sea

The Great Being alone, perfect and wondrous in penetration, enters the sea of birth and death and seals it everywhere, like the moon. Within the pure radiance the Dharma body is profoundly still; the waves of affliction may surge to the sky unchecked. The more affliction flourishes, the more the Dharma body is revealed; and so toward living beings it accords and stays near. As water holds the moon, and the moon does not leave the water, light shines upon light — there was never any this or that. I contemplate the Great Being as never apart from this mind; therefore whoever seeks responds as echo answers sound. The constant light is not obscured; death and life are not divided. Quiescence stands before one, and of oneself one transcends. (The Great Being abides as moon and water, as mind and realm: no duality at all.)
Praise of the Great Being of Empty Sea

Birth and death are like a sea; the world is like empty space. A single piece of body and mind is let go within them. Space and water mingle and merge; the waves are no longer terrible. This alone is my Teacher: true liberation.
Praise of the Manifestation in the Body of a Great Heavenly General

The gate of perfect penetration realized by all Buddhas truly enters through the six sense faculties of living beings. Though the six faculties are one and the same, they differ in depth; the ear alone is the most perfect of all. Therefore the Great Being entered by the ear gate, and, both faculty and object forgotten, even contemplation was let go. When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescence stands revealed; in a single thought one equals the Buddha and all beings. The Dharma body is equal and nothing fails to merge within it; bodies of the ten Dharma realms appear all at once. Yet each sees according to his wish, as an empty valley answers every sound. Know then that the body of a Great Heavenly General responds at once when the seeker has the mind. One body contains every body, as the sea holds the taste of a hundred rivers. The wise can contemplate apart from form and appearance, and all faculties and objects are utterly still.
Praise of the Great Being Who Subdues the Six Demons

I contemplate the Great Being, inconceivable, ever present in the bitter sea of birth and death. Body and mind alike enter every sentient being, subduing demon foes and benefiting conscious creatures. The demons are not merely eighty thousand; all take the six faculties as their bellows. When the six gates are still, the wondrous function is complete — and this is the Great Being’s awesome spiritual power. Demons and the Great Being are fundamentally not two, like empty space and the light of the sun. If space and light were different, the Great Being would be seized by demons. Therefore to bow and to call the name brings the inconceivable power forth at the very thought. The green cliff, the emerald bamboo — these are his Dharma body; thusness unmoved is true liberation.
Praise of the Great Being Who Subdues the Twelve Demons

Before the Buddha appeared in the world, the demon realm was empty; once the Buddha appeared, demons came to be. Buddha and demon are fundamentally without difference; it is only from the inverted views of living beings. When faculty and object stand opposed, the demon ramparts seal one in; when mind and realm are both forgotten, the demon hordes are destroyed. Therefore Guanyin’s wondrous power of wisdom subdues demons only by purifying faculties and objects. When the six gates stand open and the Dharma realm is empty, Buddha and demon alike no longer appear. I now bow to the Inconceivable One, praying that he bestow fearlessness on living beings, that I may at once enter the gate of perfect penetration, and that all demons may ever be my Dharma companions. When demons can raise the Dharma banner at a thought, only then is the Great Being’s awesome spiritual power felt.
Praise of the Great Being of Perfect Penetration

The Great Being’s body is nowhere absent; therefore the Great Being’s mind is perfectly penetrating and unobstructed. Living beings of the ten directions were never outside it. Blue pigment within color, a clod of earth within water: since there is no this or that, boundaries are hard to draw. So when one responds to seeking, just so is one gladdened.
Praise of the Embroidered Great Being, with a Preface

The mother of the Xia family of Jiahe, née Fan, was fifty-two years old and had kept the vegetarian fast for thirty-five years, reciting the Diamond Sutra day and night. She happened to fall ill with a fistula, and her suffering was severe. Her daughter-in-law, née Feng, was by nature perfectly filial, and vowed to take the illness upon herself. So she embroidered an image of Guanyin, for three years without slackening, and completed more than twenty scrolls. The mother’s illness indeed was cured, and her step was better than before; the daughter-in-law, however, fell ill and died. The mother thinks of her daughter-in-law’s words and laughter as if she were still alive. Her son Xishu begs that a praise be made for her. The praise says:

With unconditioned compassion his body is everywhere, entering the minds of living beings as a needle draws thread. The daughter-in-law took on her mother-in-law’s illness and embroidered the Great Being’s body; it answered as her hand moved, like shadow and form. The mother-in-law’s illness was cured, and the daughter-in-law died. This is enough to show that the essence is one: there was never any this or that. The daughter-in-law relied on the Great Being, and in death too she is not extinguished — thread by thread, line by line, she puts forth the broad and long tongue.

The Dharma body is originally without form; form follows living beings and comes to be. When the delusive thoughts of living beings arise, the Dharma body at once appears. Therefore this person of mind, recalling no other matter, fixes wholly on the wondrous Dharma body, bright and pure as undyed silk. Then with the needle of contemplation he draws along the thread of delusive thought: thought after thought pierces the Dharma body, thread after thread completes the wondrous marks. When sincerity enters the subtle and minute, not a hair’s breadth leaks away. Solemnly, upon the ground of the one true, he conjures forth the formless body, perfects the pure mind, and accomplishes the faculty of perfect penetration. Therefore I look up and rely on him, and at once enter the inconceivable.
Praise of the Embroidered Great Being Crossing the Sea

In the sea of the three poisons, when the waves are at their worst, he walks upon the crown of his head and his feet stay perfectly dry. Entering the minds of living beings, he is nowhere absent; from a thread of delusive thought the Dharma body appears. Thought after thought is not in vain, mind after mind must pierce through. The universal gate reveals itself, and of itself it is accomplished.
Praise of the Thousand-Armed Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, with a Preface

The layman Zheng Fa of Goulou, through the conditions of past habit, bowed single-mindedly in reverence to the Thousand-Armed Bodhisattva of Great Compassion, holding the sacred mantra in his heart, diligent and unwearied for many years, hoping to rely on the awesome spirit and accomplish it within one lifetime. He reflected that all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas save living beings by no fixed method: as one drowning in the great sea, whatever he finds to cling to, he will surely reach the farther shore; and as the many grasses of the snowy mountains are all of them medicine. Know then that if a living being can wish to escape birth and death, whether he practices Chan, recites the Buddha’s name, holds mantras, or reads sutras, so long as he can truly believe in his own mind and stand firm without retreating, there is none who will not escape birth and death — how much more when he relies on the power of the Great Being’s same-essence great compassion and the power of the sacred mantra? How could it not be accomplished in one lifetime? The layman came to Mount Kuang to consult this old man for instruction; since there was no Dharma to speak, I made this praise and gave it to him. If one understands the purport that light and darkness are not two, then the paths of sage and ordinary being are cut off, and the feelings of birth and death wither. Then, in daily use, in every instance and in every hair’s pore, all is the time of the Great Being’s hands and eyes, blazing with radiance. The layman should contemplate in this way: the one mind is complete in itself and borrows nothing from outside. The praise says:

The afflictions of living beings number eighty-four thousand; because of darkness they revolve through the six paths. In the Great Being’s body they become hands and eyes; the radiance of every hair’s pore turns along with the darkness. Therefore when living beings have suffering they must call out; the answer comes with the call, and the darkness is suddenly gone. Living beings and the Great Being were never two things: light comes and darkness goes, and it appears at the very thought. All the wise seek only within themselves; the two paths of ordinary being and sage were never this or that. As a lamp breaks the darkness, neither reaches the other; because they are not two, one sees the wonder. If one can contemplate thus, the Great Being is oneself; to bow and hold the name is as water entering water. Only take the suffering of beings at its utmost and lift it up: radiance shines forth, undiminished day and night.
Praise of the Four-Armed Guanyin

Hands and eyes filling the whole body — why only four? Within the inexhaustible he lets it be merely thus. The jewel scepter empties demons; the true sutra has no words. All of it is spiritual power, an inconceivable matter.
In Reverence to the Great Being, the Tathagata in the Sky

The Tathagata in the sky, whence does he appear? Just at this moment he stands face to face with the Great Being. Having become Buddha long ago, why bow to another? By revealing him one reveals oneself. After all, how is it? Manifestation is not one; bowing and mindfulness are not two. He universally manifests a physical body — truly inconceivable.
Praise of the Great Being of the Fire-Light Samadhi

The light of prajna is like a towering blaze; within it the Great Being enters the ground of coolness. The afflictions of living beings are themselves this prajna light; therefore the Great Being’s wondrous response is without fixed direction.
Praise of Bodhisattva Jeweled Palm

Asked who he was, he called himself Jeweled Palm; he stretched his hand and brushed the sky, and suddenly it gave a sound. What is heard in an empty sound? What is touched when the hand brushes? Should he meet a venomous dragon, he could not draw his hand back in time.
Praise of Cundi Bodhisattva

I have heard that the place where all Buddhas are born comes from the subtle and secret seal. The secret seal is the mind of all Buddhas, scattered into the delusive dreams of living beings. If the dreams are shattered, the Buddhas appear, as sunlight is seen in the cold sky; if the clouds of living beings’ afflictions are shattered, it is revealed by reliance on the Tathagata’s secret mantra power. To hold the mantra is to hold the mind of all Buddhas; my own mind was originally the secret mantra. The meeting of the three conditions is fundamentally not two; therefore a single thought is wholly complete. If only one can keep it ever present in daily use, like a child who, having found its mother, will not leave her — the Buddha-mind has already entered the mantra-holding mind, and one need not seek the Buddha to be liberated of oneself.
Praise of Bodhisattva Sunlight, with a Preface

Guangfu Temple on Guanyin Mountain, east of the town of Qu’e, was founded by a divine monk of the Song, who was named Bodhisattva Sunlight. The Bodhisattva first appeared as an elder monk of contrary conduct who paid no heed to the precepts, and his contemporaries despised him; when they further reproached him for building a monastery, he appeared in body in place after place and gathered alms all at once, so that those who went looking for his traces found he had still not left the temple gate. All quarters were moved and thought him strange, and so a precious monastery was completed. At the end of his life he revealed his own name, and to this day he is called Bodhisattva Sunlight. The temple fell into ruin; its abbot Tong Ta restored it anew, set up an image and enshrined it, and asked me for a praise. The praise says:

The sun alone in the sky shines bright and clear; mountain and river, deep valley — there is no place it does not light. Defilement cannot muddy it, fair weather cannot dim it. It is like a reflection in water, like a trace within a shadow. The mind that dwells in living beings is supremely divine and spiritual; it is not two with the Buddha — how much less so in a monk? The lotus rises from the mud, fragrant and pure, unstained; the mani jewel lies in filth, its radiance undiminished. Therefore the perfected one transcends and is utterly free of defilement; he does not dwell in the body — how could he be bound by ordinary or sage? He breaks the rules of deportment and shows himself at play. Fleshly eyes cling to appearances and do not know who he is. He does not leave his courtyard, yet his body fills the ten directions; he was never coming or going — like the light of the sun. Even one born blind relies on it to do his work. Adornment of form and appearance is still but spittle; his traces are like space, his response like the wind. He reveals himself wherever he is, and without appointment all is the same. One day is a thousand ages; one mind is ten thousand kalpas. Therefore the Great Being’s spirit is never exhausted.
Praise of Vimalakirti at Play in the Garden

He does not see a Pure Land, and so does not love to dwell there; he does not see a defiled land, and so does not loathe to live there. Monk or layman? A form to be seen: is it real or empty? Men and women mingled together: is it so or not? His mouth is vast as space, his tongue vast as his mouth; he does not know how to preach the Dharma, so he hides his shame in silence. His body is not ill, yet by illness he makes his body ill. Were this not borrowed play, it would be enough to make one die of laughter. Manjushri had not yet come, and so he arranged and waited; when at last he arrived, it was a whole debacle. For a thousand ages he has been duped, and those who see him measure and reckon. It is not the World-Honored One — hard indeed to grope for. The thirty-two were all made sport of. Luckily there was Manjushri, idly tearing and teasing. I do not know him, and he does not know me; let us wait until Maitreya is born, and when it is seen through, only then will the crowd disperse.
Praise of the Venerable Kaundinya

The elephant king roams abroad, and the elephant calf follows after. Like calls to like; meeting conditions, they gather. Though the enmity between them was heaviest, in the Way they are the closest kin. As two carts make the same ruts, surely there is a cause.
Praise of the Portraits of the Thirty-Three Patriarchs
The First Patriarch, the Venerable Mahakasyapa

A golden-hued form, a diamond heart; he upheld the wisdom-life and ever turned the Dharma wheel. When the World-Honored One twirled the flower, he broke into a smile — and to this day it leaves people unable to conceive or speak of it.
The Second Patriarch, the Venerable Ananda

His vast learning was like the sea, drinking in and drawing up the stream of Dharma. All Buddhas, as they come and go, never leave his tongue. He blows the reed-pipe of Dharma transformation, and beat by beat it becomes a command. Therefore my Teacher is the one who is the true within the partial.
The Third Patriarch, the Venerable Sanakavasa

His prajna root had been realized in a former life; therefore when the Master was about to appear, the auspicious grass first answered. Mind seals mind, as fire casts into fire; meeting on a narrow path, there is surely nowhere to hide.
The Fourth Patriarch, the Venerable Upagupta

When one man’s mind becomes empty, the demon palaces tremble. Grasping the diamond blade, who dares trifle with him? If he would but turn the light around, the wild mind is stilled in an instant; bowing in refuge, all his transgressions are wiped away.
The Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Nadi-Daśika

He had already awakened to the original mind, as sunlight shines through night. He shows the dream of birth and death, and his radiance surpasses it. The Master’s Dharma was originally nothing; my mind does not exist. As space meets space, his tongue never leaves his mouth.
The Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Michaka

For this alone he came; for no other matter. Meeting in the bustling market, he reveals his own vessel of himself. The prefect saw what had not yet come to be, and knew this day beforehand. When one is to do business, one does not haggle over the price.
The Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Vasumitra

He came by a familiar road and suddenly met a friend and kin. In a single word they discussed the truth, and at once he knew what he had not had before. He begged for the taste of sweet dew, and the Master showed him the Dharma of emptiness. If one claims to have gained something, he falls in with seven, falls in with eight.
The Eighth Patriarch, the Venerable Buddhanandi

It is not that he does not speak — it is that speech cannot reach it. It is not that he does not act — there was never any trace. Now that he has met the right man, only then may he open his mouth. From there he simply goes on, and does not fall into the old ruts.
The Ninth Patriarch, the Venerable Buddhamitra

He dwelt in his mother’s womb for sixty years, waiting only for the Master to come and so fulfill the former cause. The radiance on his crown was originally his own; let it be scraped once and it shines through — like a lion’s roar.
The Tenth Patriarch, the Venerable Pārśva

He pointed at the ground and it turned to gold, appearing at the movement of his hand. The sage at once drew near — what ease, what swiftness! He is like an empty valley that answers every sound with an echo. Know then that my own mind was never coming or going.
The Eleventh Patriarch, the Venerable Punyayaśas

The Buddha does not know the Buddha; the eye does not see the eye. To seek further from another — and so he met with reproof. He thought himself whole and complete, but was seen through long before. Waking with a start, only then did he know his words had fallen flat.
The Twelfth Patriarch, the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa

The horse’s mournful cry had a cause of its own. The woman who rose from the earth was not the right person after all. The demon was never a demon, nor the Buddha a Buddha. Looked at with the true eye, what thing is he in the end?
The Thirteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kapimala

He came from among the heterodox and attained right knowledge and view. Meeting a venomous snake on the road, his compassionate mind appeared. When further he questioned the venomous dragon, both were brought to submission. What the eye sees and the mind knows is like an echo issuing from the valley.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Nāgārjuna

A dragon among dragons, meeting poison with poison. The Venerable Master’s wondrous hand subdued them with a single word. The samadhi of Buddha-nature is in essence like empty space; a hundred thousand Dharma gates all enter within it.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kanadeva

He dropped a needle into the bowl, wondrously matching the wordless. He revealed the meaning of Buddha-nature, and the full moon appeared before him. Coming to the elder’s house, he used the needle to draw thread: borrowing another’s causal conditions as expedient means for himself.
The Sixteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Rāhulata

Following the stream, he found the source; where the water ended and the mountains ran out, he suddenly met the man and knew him for a sage. Fragrant rice was lifted up and offered, and they shared seats and food. The great assembly drank together, and the sweet dew was like honey.
The Seventeenth Patriarch, the Venerable Saṅghanandi

He took no delight in the royal palace, and heaven opened a single road. Going straight to the exhausted source, he did not know the reason why. Beneath the purple clouds was where the sage dwelt; and in the end he found the boy, who met the profound intent of all Buddhas.
The Eighteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Gayāśata

Born after seven days, he did not fall into the aggregates. His body was fragrant and pure, originally clean. At a single word spoken at the door — “Who is it that answers nothing?” — he was suddenly startled awake, and in that instant knew where to return.
The Nineteenth Patriarch, the Venerable Kumāralāta

Having been born in heaven, he should not have given rise to desire. One thought not yet forgotten, and he was no longer at ease. By the power of prajna he rose again to the Brahma world; so he came to transmit the lamp — that was his family affair.
The Twentieth Patriarch, the Venerable Jayata

The unborn is inherently complete; there is no need to seek the truth. It arises when it meets conditions, as a flower meets spring. Seek it too urgently, and you turn farther from the Way. Know where to return in this instant, and come back along the very road.
The Twenty-First Patriarch, the Venerable Vasubandhu

Light and darkness share one essence; sage and ordinary being are one road. His place of coming was hidden and subtle, and none knew the reason. What is familiar is hard to forget, so he sought a companion further. Suddenly they met, and his willing mind gave its own consent.
The Twenty-Second Patriarch, the Venerable Manorhita

From the time of his prediction he came for no other matter. Like joins with like, and meeting conditions they must encounter each other. Alas, those cranes — they had flown and cried for long; at a single word, he knew at once what he had always had.
The Twenty-Third Patriarch, the Venerable Haklenayaśas

From the summit of Mount Sumeru he brought a golden ring. Alas, those cranes — their plight was pitiable. He got himself a lion cub who gave a great roar; its spirit pierced the heavens, and by it his heirs were tested.
The Twenty-Fourth Patriarch, the Monk Simha

When they met he asked for the pearl, and with an open hand it was there. What had been entrusted before had not long been parted. Knowing there was an old debt, he came expressly to repay it. With his head laid on the blade, white milk flowed out.
The Twenty-Fifth Patriarch, the Venerable Vasiṣṭha

Wielding the sword of prajna and holding the wish-fulfilling pearl, though he came only for a while, this journey was not in vain. By chance he met a wicked man and found in him a fine companion; through the crooked he struck the straight, and both had their advantage.
The Twenty-Sixth Patriarch, the Venerable Punyamitra

From the kshatriya caste he continued the transmission of the lamp’s flame. His true heir was not clear, and he nearly came to ruin; in the bustling market he suddenly met his old friend, and case fitting lid, he got the true one.
The Twenty-Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Prajñātārā

Do not say there was no cause: meeting, he saw at once. His place of coming was natural, without resort to expedients. Now by means of that pearl he found the right man — digging a pond, he got the moon; buying stones, he got more than clouds.
The Twenty-Eighth Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma

The Master’s mind was in great haste, and he came too early. Not a single word struck home, and his mind was not yet settled. He sat coldly in Shaolin; then he was fortunate to get Shenguang, who lost an arm — and his Way has flourished ever since.
The Twenty-Ninth Patriarch, the Great Master Huike

He came by sea expressly, with how much bitter toil. Within the land of the Great Tang he found only one man. Seeking it, one cannot find it; it is as water taking the shape of the vessel. By this he passed on the family tradition, and so he is the Second.
The Thirtieth Patriarch, the Great Master Sengcan

His whole body was an illness, and he did not know whence it came. Then he suddenly met the King of Physicians and woke with a start to its cause. With mind empty and bones firm he simply took to the road; meeting one of great strength, he handed over the whole load.
The Thirty-First Patriarch, the Great Master Daoxin

He left home while young, of sharp and swift faculties. For more than sixty years his side never touched a mat. Students gathered like clouds; why wait for a child? Because there was a former agreement, though those who looked on did not know it.
The Thirty-Second Patriarch, the Great Master Hongren

His origins were unclear, yet his birth was just right. One matter left unfinished, and both families were settled. In the mountains of Potou, on the road to Huangmei, he came and went freely, bearing the marks of a great man.
The Thirty-Third Patriarch, the Great Master Huineng

He had just thrown down the woodcutter’s axe; a stone was tied to his waist. The root of wisdom had long been planted, and from this it put forth shoots. Its source flows out from Caoxi and runs across the whole earth; to this very day there is no place it is not.
Praise of the Eighteen Arhats, with a Preface

In former days Li Longmian drew the eighteen arhats in fine ink outline, exquisite and inspired, dazzling the eyes of all who saw. Only Zhao Songxue could imitate them and come close to life. In recent times Ding Nanyu of Shexian painted the portraits of the patriarchs and did not yield to the ancients, and his fine outline work too was reckoned excellent. I once asked him to paint a “Crossing and Lifting the Robe” picture, but never obtained it. Lately, in Wuyang, Lord Hou of Nanhai and my friend Wang brought out this scroll and asked for a praise. Unrolled, its radiance dazzles the eye and its spirit and manner surpass the ordinary, as though one were sitting within the Lotus Treasury, hearing the Tathagata teach the Dharma gate of self-nature. On asking who the painter was, it proved to be the student Wang Boyu of Huangmei. Reverently burning incense and bowing my head, I made a praise for the whole of it. The praise says:

Within the realm of purity all wonders are born; the great earth and its mountains and rivers all return to perfect illumination. Fish and shell, feather and fur universally manifest samadhi — why should the arhats alone be thought a rare matter? All the arhats are phantom bodies; seeing them without recognizing them, how can one get their truth? At play in spiritual powers, they cough and spit, shake their arms; they bow and lift, bend and stretch — all are Buddha-work. A lion yawns and groans, or gathers his spirit in wall-gazing; beneath the trees, beside the water, his livelihood is beyond reckoning. Clenching a fist, the hand grows sore; subduing a dragon takes effort. Only let the deluded mind rest, and of itself all is silent and still. Hugging his knees and gazing fixedly, watching the other play his tricks — better to hold the beads and recite the Buddha’s name at ease. Belly bared and beaming, a palm-leaf scripture in his hand; he waves a whisk and talks in silence, striking emptiness so that it sounds. The listener is as though deaf, the speaker as though mute — not like the ordinary man with all his “thees” and “thous.” Weary, he leans on a tall pine, nodding and dozing; he stretches out his hand into space and is suddenly startled awake. Bones thin, brows long, waist bent, legs straight — every step he takes depends wholly on the power that bears him up. Sitting at ease in the quiet of the woods, his mind is idle beyond measure; now and then he looks at a sutra, and at once his words fall flat. One bowl, seven scrolls of the lotus — just this is the treasure; what need of other things? Where he finds his own use, this and nothing more. Dragons and gods revere him, and he takes no joy in it. Let others love or hate, let them bind him as they will: he savors one flavor of following conditions, and his self-nature is liberated. Only at the tip of a hair he manifests this spiritual power: the trace of a fish in the depths, the track of a bird in the air, a form in a mirror, a flower in the sky, a castle in the clouds, the moon in water. Contemplate thus — its wonder cannot be spoken.

The karmic consciousness is not dried up, and they drift upon the sea of poison — fish and turtle, crocodile and dragon, yaksha and ghost and monster. Laughable, you lot! You ride on emptiness with one flavor, not daring to fall in with their kind, and call it spiritual power. Bitterly you are rebuked by the Buddha, and afraid to face Vimalakirti; luckily for you, here you are at leisure and have dodged Huangbo. Vast the long swell, surging the mighty waves — you will not let your body go. What manner of thing is that? You take the dry land for yourself and make others go into the water; even if that is a bargain, how long can it last? Though called a game, in the end it turns to emptiness and deceit. Called and called, you will not turn your head back, and my melancholy only deepens. I shall watch you struggle on until the Dragon Flower Assembly comes. What sort of nose will you show when you meet my own Teacher, the monk?
Further, a Combined Praise in Sequence

Each holds a single sutra, and all of them lie before the eyes; the roads differ, but supporting a household is the same. Squatting on the ground he sits, both eyes staring into space. What has he seen, to set up this style of gate? Beneath the cliff he takes a stump for a bench; the incense spiral rises into the void like clouds making rain. His bones are thin as firewood, his spirit already spent, and still he must read the sutra, and his mind will not rest. His back itches and is hard to scratch, so he idly borrows a hand; where it lands is just the right place, and its wonder cannot be told. What spiritual power has he, hiding a dragon in a bottle? Loosen the hand and let it out, and let it soar as it will. A fierce tiger crouches on the ground, its majesty not to be touched; he exhausts all his strength, like a cat catching a mouse. The sutra is not words, and no few bear it: do not say that the eyes are weary and drowsiness is no good. A sound is made in the ear, as though there were some thing; and when you reach for it, you cannot get it out. The bright moon is in the sky, and he sits hugging his knees. Such leisure — what joy! His long brows hang heavy and keep veiling his eyes; his old hands have no strength, and turning the scroll costs him dear. His belly is too big to hide, and a fine sloven he looks; only let it go, and he is light and quick. In a patched and faded robe, he takes pains to mend it piece by piece; every stitch and every thread, such hardship. Holding a bright mirror, he sees his own ugliness; then he meets a lion, and it gives a single roar. They cross the water together, heels to the very bottom — what need is there to burden others, to burden ghosts?
Further, a Combined Praise on the Picture of Play in the Garden

My Teacher’s spiritual power — of himself he has limited store, and relies wholly on everyone, heads together and faces gathered. A dragon cannot be tamed; on this one bowl they rely — were it not for these, they would draw in hand and foot. The hand counts the prayer beads, and by this feigns reciting the Buddha’s name; giving up oneself to follow others only shows up the muddle. Holding a single stick of incense, whom does he make offering to? Conditioned merit is not as good as the unconditioned. Raised fists and clasped palms exchange mutual respect; facing the mirror he sees a head, and empty sound answers the valley. His hand holds the wish-fulfilling jewel — it was not without intent; look at what there was before he held it. Turn the head sharply — why keep looking back? To wait for a companion to walk with one is no longer a bold stride. Within the water vessel no pouring is seen; one thinks it must be glass holding sweet dew inside. In youth he did not strive, in age his mind is not at rest; he raises his brows and still must read the sutra. Seen from my side, all of this is a display of folly: though he can ride the clouds, he has not left the old nest. Those before have gone, those behind have not yet come; unable to keep pace, he cannot help but brood. He walks quickly and cannot move — fearing the sky will rain, he first puts on a bamboo hat, adding hardship to hardship. The palm-leaf leaves are without writing, the true sutra is without words; he only understands reciting with the mouth and does not know the mind’s awakening. Because the other has dust, he holds the white whisk; that one is pure and this one defiled, and both are wanting. Raised fists and clasped palms, walking together or going alone — look at his wish-fulfilling jewel: it is just right for scratching an itch. The head of the white feather fan is pure as snow; he has already cut off affliction, so why is he still hot? Let him ask the bowl whether there is any rice in it: if hunger comes, the donor will provide. A fierce tiger’s claws and fangs open a bloody mouth; fortunately it met my Teacher, and was tamed and went off. A single scroll of the true sutra holds immeasurable meaning; before it is unrolled, he has already seen the truth. All these many games are empty and deceitful; just look at empty space — what manner of thing is it?
Further, a Praise on the Picture of Crossing the Sea

The sea of suffering is boundless, and the wicked waves beat the sky; he crosses straight over, body laid across — who dares be first? Only the Venerable Ones, at ease in their spiritual powers, stake their lives without a thought and go on and take no harm. Because I am empty, nothing harms me; within and without there is nothing, and so there is nothing to cast off. They look on the abyss as a ridge, and tread the perilous as level; they arrive as their minds wish, and their eyes rest on it unalarmed. Though there be crocodiles, yakshas, ghosts and monsters, all are used by me, because I am utterly beyond opposites. Know then that the perfected one, dwelling amid birth and death, does not contend with things, and no thing fails to receive him. Seen in this light, the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent: only do not give rise to a mind, and it is called perfection beyond compare.
Further, a Praise of Each According to His Posture
One figure raises a vajra tower in his right hand, while his left palm is held upright as though engaged in contemplation.
With the vajra tower he gives some token of this mind; the upright palm and close contemplation — the thought and remembrance are profound.
